title: Straits: Narrow Passages Between Seas
summary: What a strait is, why these narrow waterways matter so much for shipping and the global economy, and why countries pay close attention to key straits such as the Strait of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb near Arabia.
poll: A narrow strait can be more important to world trade than a wide ocean.

versions.title: Straits: Narrow Passages Between Seas
versions.text:
Look at a map of the world. You will see seas. You will see oceans. Some of them touch.

What joins them? A strait does. A strait is not a road. It is a strip of water. It is narrow.

A strait connects two big seas. Ships use it. A ship can go through. This saves time.

Many ships use one strait. It can get busy. This makes the strait important for trade.

To trade is to send goods. Ships carry oil. Ships carry food. Ships carry other things too.

One strait is near Arabia. Its name is Hormuz. Many ships pass through it.

Another strait is near Arabia too. Its name is Bab-el-Mandeb. Ships use it as well.

If a strait shuts, ships cannot pass. Goods must go a long way. Costs can go up.

A strait joins seas. It helps ships. It helps trade all over the world.

versions.title: Straits: Narrow Passages Between Seas
versions.text:
Look at a map of the world. You will see many seas. You will see oceans too. In some spots, two of them almost touch.

What joins them there? A strait does. A strait is not a road. It is a narrow strip of water. It connects two bigger seas.

Ships use straits to go from one sea to the next. They do not go the long way around land. This can save many days.

Many ships use the same narrow strait. It can get very busy. This makes straits important for trade.

Trade means sending goods from one place to another. Ships that use straits carry oil, food, cars, and other goods.

One famous strait is near Arabia. It is called the Strait of Hormuz. A lot of oil moves through it each day.

Another strait near Arabia is called Bab-el-Mandeb. It joins the Red Sea to a sea close by. Many ships use it too.

If a strait were closed, ships could not pass through it. Goods would have to go a much longer way. Prices could go up.

Straits join seas. They help ships move fast. They help keep trade going all over the world.

versions.title: Straits: Narrow Passages Between Seas
versions.text:
If you look closely at a map, you will see that some seas almost touch. In a few spots, only a thin strip of water lies between them.

That strip of water is a strait. A strait is not a road. It is a narrow passage of water. It connects two bigger seas.

Ships use straits to travel between seas. They skip the long way around land. A trip that took many days can take just a few hours.

So many ships use the same narrow strait. It can become a very busy spot. This makes straits important for trade.

Trade is giving goods for other goods or money. Ships that pass through straits carry oil, food, cars, and other things people need.

One famous strait lies near Arabia. It is called the Strait of Hormuz. A large share of the world's oil ships through it each day.

Another strait close to Arabia is Bab-el-Mandeb. It joins the Red Sea to a nearby sea. Many cargo ships pass through it too.

If a strait were ever closed, ships could not pass through. Goods would travel a much longer way. Prices could rise around the world.

Straits join seas. They help ships travel fast. They help keep trade moving across the whole world.

versions.title: Straits: Narrow Passages Between Seas
versions.text:
Long before airplanes, sailors knew a strait could save many days at sea. A strait is a narrow natural waterway. It joins two bigger seas, letting ships pass from one into the other.

Straits matter because of geography. A ship sailing from one sea to another can pass through a strait, instead of going all the way around a whole continent. This saves time, fuel, and money.

Because so much traffic uses one narrow route, a strait can quickly become one of the busiest waterways on Earth. Many cargo ships pass through major straits each day, carrying oil, clothes, and other goods.

This heavy traffic makes straits vital to the economy. Countries depend on this steady cargo to keep stores stocked and fuel prices stable. If a strait is blocked, even briefly, the effects can reach far-off markets.

Near Arabia, two straits stand out. The Strait of Hormuz links the Arabian Gulf to the Arabian Sea. A huge share of the world's oil travels this route. Farther south, Bab-el-Mandeb links the Red Sea to another sea nearby.

Other famous straits link far-off parts of the world. The Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia and Indonesia, is a very busy shipping route. The Bosphorus, in Turkey, links two seas as well.

Because straits are so narrow, storms can sometimes close them. This can slow trade for whole regions. For this reason, laws protect the right of ships to use busy straits.

Straits look small on a map, but their narrow waters carry a huge share of world trade, making them some of the most important waterways on Earth.

Straits matter largely because of geography. Because so much traffic funnels through one narrow route, a strait can rapidly become what analysts call a chokepoint, a single narrow place through which a large share of trade must pass.

A strait that works as a chokepoint can also become a bottleneck. Even a brief disruption there can delay cargo meant for ports far away. Thousands of cargo vessels and oil tankers pass through major straits every day, carrying crude oil and electronics.

This heavy traffic renders straits vital to the economy. Nations depend on steady cargo through these waterways to keep factories operating and fuel prices stable. Near the Arabian Peninsula, two straits stand out: the Strait of Hormuz links the Arabian Gulf to the Arabian Sea, and much of the world's oil travels this route aboard tankers. Farther south, Bab-el-Mandeb links the Red Sea to another sea nearby.

Other renowned straits link very different parts of the world. The Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia and Indonesia, is one of the busiest shipping routes anywhere. The Bosphorus, in Turkey, links two seas through the heart of a major city.

Because they are so narrow, straits also carry strategic weight that goes beyond ordinary trade. A country that controls a major strait often holds real geopolitical influence, since the power to affect traffic through a chokepoint can shape ties between distant nations.

Straits can occasionally close because of storms, accidents, or conflict, slowing trade across whole regions overnight. This is why international law protects the right of vessels to pass through straits peacefully.

Straits may look small on a map, but their narrow waters carry an enormous share of global trade, making them among the most strategically important waterways on the entire planet.

versions.text:
Long before airplanes existed, mariners understood that a strait could save many days at sea. A strait is a slender natural waterway connecting two larger seas, permitting vessels to pass from one sea into another without circumnavigating an entire continent.

Straits matter largely because of geography. Because so much traffic funnels through one constricted route, a strait can rapidly become what analysts term a chokepoint, a single narrow location through which a disproportionately large share of trade must pass.

A strait functioning as a chokepoint can also become a bottleneck, since even a brief disruption there can delay cargo destined for ports thousands of kilometers away. Thousands of cargo vessels and oil tankers traverse major straits every single day, transporting crude petroleum and electronics.

This heavy traffic renders straits vital to the economy, since nations depend on steady cargo through these waterways to keep factories operating and fuel prices stable. Because they are so narrow, straits also carry strategic weight that extends beyond ordinary trade. A country that controls a major strait often wields considerable geopolitical influence, since the power to affect traffic through a chokepoint can shape ties between distant nations and even shift the balance of trade for entire regions.

Straits may look insignificant on a map, but their narrow waters carry a disproportionately large share of global trade, which makes them among the most strategically important waterways on the entire planet.

Long before airplanes existed, mariners understood that a strait could save many days at sea. A strait is a slender natural waterway connecting two larger seas, permitting vessels to pass from one sea into another without circumnavigating an entire continent and its surrounding coastline.

Straits matter largely because of geography. Because so much shipping traffic funnels through one constricted route, a strait can rapidly become what analysts term a chokepoint, a singular narrow location through which a disproportionately large share of global commerce must pass.

A strait functioning as a chokepoint can also become a bottleneck, since even a transient disruption there can delay cargo destined for ports thousands of kilometers distant. This incessant traffic renders straits vital to the economy, since nations depend on an uninterrupted flow of cargo through these waterways to keep factories operating and fuel prices stable. Other renowned straits link vastly different regions of the globe. A nation that controls a major strait often wields considerable geopolitical influence, since the capacity to affect traffic through a chokepoint can shape relationships between distant nations, sometimes for generations at a time.

Straits can occasionally close because of violent storms, accidents, or armed conflict, interrupting trade across entire regions almost overnight, which is why international maritime law safeguards the right of vessels to pass through straits peacefully.

Straits may appear insignificant on a map, but their narrow waters carry a disproportionately large share of global trade, which renders them among the most strategically important waterways on the entire planet.

Because they are inherently narrow, straits also carry strategic weight that extends well beyond ordinary commerce into the realm of international relations. versions.text:
Long before airplanes existed, mariners understood that some of the fastest conceivable paths between two seas were never located in open water at all, but rather within narrow passages known as straits. A strait is a slender natural waterway connecting two substantially larger seas, permitting vessels to pass from one into another without circumnavigating an entire continent and its surrounding coastline.

Straits matter largely because of underlying geography. Because so much shipping traffic funnels through one constricted route, a strait can rapidly become what analysts and economists term a chokepoint, a singular narrow location through which a disproportionately large share of global commerce must inevitably pass.

A strait functioning as a chokepoint can also become a severe bottleneck, since even a transient disruption there can delay cargo destined for ports thousands of kilometers distant, rippling outward through intricate supply chains across multiple continents simultaneously. Thousands of cargo vessels and oil tankers traverse major straits every single day, transporting crude petroleum and sophisticated electronics without meaningful interruption.

This incessant traffic renders straits absolutely vital to the economy, since nations depend overwhelmingly on an uninterrupted flow of cargo through these waterways to keep factories operating and fuel prices relatively stable worldwide. Near the Arabian Peninsula, two straits stand out: the Strait of Hormuz links the Arabian Gulf to the Arabian Sea, and much of the entire world's traded oil travels this precise route aboard enormous tankers, while Bab-el-Mandeb, farther south, links the Red Sea to another sea nearby.

Other renowned straits link vastly different regions of the globe. The Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia and Indonesia, remains one of the busiest shipping routes anywhere on the entire Earth, while the Bosphorus, in Turkey, links two seas through the very heart of a sprawling metropolis. The Strait of Gibraltar, between Spain and Morocco, links the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean and has shaped trade and travel between two continents for many centuries.

Because they are inherently narrow, straits also carry strategic weight that extends well beyond ordinary commerce into the delicate realm of international relations. A nation that controls a major strait often wields considerable geopolitical influence, since the capacity to affect traffic through a chokepoint can shape relationships between distant nations and even influence energy markets and diplomatic negotiations for decades at a stretch.

Straits can occasionally close because of violent storms, maritime accidents, or armed conflict, interrupting trade across entire regions almost overnight, which is precisely why international maritime law safeguards the right of vessels to pass through straits peacefully.

Straits may appear insignificant on an ordinary map, but their narrow waters carry a disproportionately large share of global trade, which renders them among the most strategically important waterways on the entire planet.

MID.prompt: The article explains that straits are vital to the economy. Why do you think a narrow waterway can be so important? Use at least two details from the article to explain.
checklist: I gave a clear answer to the question.
I supported my answer with at least two details from the article.
I used words such as waterway, cargo, or route correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: A narrow waterway can be extremely important because so much cargo depends on using the shortest route between two seas. For example, the article explains that a ship can pass through a strait instead of sailing all the way around a continent, saving huge amounts of time and fuel. Because so many ships rely on the same route, blocking even one strait can affect the economy of countries far away.

keyWords.definition: a narrow place through which an unusually large share of traffic or trade must pass
keyWords.example: The single bridge into the city became a chokepoint during rush hour.

keyWords.definition: having to do with how geography affects politics and power between countries
keyWords.example: The island's location gave it geopolitical importance far beyond its small size.

keyWords.definition: a large ship built to carry liquids such as oil in great quantities
keyWords.example: A massive tanker sat anchored near the port, waiting to unload its oil.

keyWords.definition: important for long-term plans, power, or advantage
keyWords.example: The general chose the hill because of its strategic position overlooking the valley.

keyWords.definition: a narrow point that slows down or limits the flow of something
keyWords.example: The single checkout lane created a bottleneck at the busy store.

HIGH.prompt: Some people argue that controlling a chokepoint gives a country outsized power. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.

I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that controlling a chokepoint can give a country outsized power. The article also notes that disrupting a strait can create a bottleneck that delays cargo across entire supply chains, showing how a small stretch of water can carry strategic weight far beyond its size.
